questions.question: circleArea, rectangleArea, and isPassingGrade all count as pure. What do they have in common that makes this true?
options: They are all short, one-line definitions.
They all return a numeric type.
Each one's result depends only on its supplied arguments, and evaluating it causes no outside-world effect.
They are all defined using the keyword pure.
questions.explanation: Purity is defined by two conditions in this lesson: same inputs always give the same output, and evaluation causes no secret interaction with the outside world. Length, return type, and keywords are irrelevant to the definition.
optionFeedback: Length is incidental. A much longer function can still be pure, and a one-line function can still be impure if it prints or reads something.
isPassingGrade returns Bool, not a number, so this cannot be the shared property — and return type has nothing to do with purity anyway.
Correct. This is exactly the two-part definition of purity: determinism from inputs, and no side effect during evaluation.
Haskell has no `pure` keyword for marking ordinary functions this way; purity is a property the function happens to have, not a declared modifier.

questions.question: if score >= 50 then "Pass" else "Fail" is described as an expression rather than a statement. What is the actual, structural reason Haskell's if requires an else?
options: Style convention only — GHC would accept it without else, but the course discourages it
The whole if...then...else construct is an expression, and an expression must produce a value on whichever branch runs; without else there would be no value for the False case
else is only required when the branches return different types
Haskell requires else so that the condition is evaluated twice, once per branch
questions.explanation: The lesson states this directly: 'Both produce values. That is why Haskell's if requires an else: the entire expression must have a result whichever branch is chosen.' This is a structural requirement of expressions having types, not a style preference.
optionFeedback: This is not a style convention GHC merely prefers — omitting else is rejected before the program runs, because the expression would have no value on the False path.
Correct. Every expression must have a type, and a type comes from the value produced; a missing else leaves the False case with no value at all.
The requirement holds even when both branches would return the exact same type — it is about needing a value on every path, not about a type mismatch between branches.
The condition is evaluated once, to pick a branch; else has nothing to do with how many times the condition itself is checked.

questions.question: In doubleAll, what job does map actually do?
options: It sorts the list before doubling it.
It applies double to every element of the list and collects the results into a new list, in order.
It removes duplicate elements from the list.
It mutates numbers in place, replacing each element with its double.
questions.explanation: map takes a one-argument function and a list, and produces a new list where that function has been applied to every element — nothing about sorting, deduplicating, or in-place mutation.
optionFeedback: Nothing about map involves ordering; doubleAll [3,1,2] would give [6,2,4] — same order as the input, not sorted.
Correct. This is exactly the reusable pattern named in the lesson: apply one function to every element.
map never removes anything from the list; the output list has exactly as many elements as the input.
numbers is never touched. doubleAll produces a brand-new list; the original binding, if it had a name elsewhere, would be completely unaffected.

questions.question: After evaluating discountedRate, what is the value of taxRate?
options: 0.12, because discountedRate overwrote it
0.14, unchanged — exactly what it was defined as
It becomes undefined, because it was used to build another value
It depends on the order the two names are evaluated in
questions.explanation: discountedRate reads taxRate's value to compute its own; reading is not writing. taxRate keeps meaning 0.14 in its scope no matter how many other definitions refer to it.
optionFeedback: This treats = as an imperative assignment that discountedRate's definition somehow performs on taxRate. Haskell's = never works that way — nothing here writes to taxRate.
Correct. taxRate is bound once, and every expression that mentions it — including discountedRate's own definition — simply reads that one fixed value.
A binding does not become 'used up' or undefined by being referenced elsewhere. taxRate remains a perfectly ordinary, still-defined name.
Haskell's immutable bindings do not have an evaluation order that could change the outcome here; taxRate means 0.14 regardless of when or how often it is read.

check-pure-functions-and-side-effects.title: Check: pure functions and side effects

questions.question: In the daysRemaining example, which single line is the effect?
options: daysRemaining today examDay = examDay - today
main = print (daysRemaining 100 130)
Both lines are effects, since main uses daysRemaining
Neither line is an effect; Haskell programs have no effects until IO is imported
questions.explanation: print is what actually touches the terminal. daysRemaining just subtracts two already-known numbers — a pure calculation that produces a value, not an action.
optionFeedback: This is ordinary subtraction on two supplied Integer values. It produces a result; it does not interact with anything outside itself.
Correct. print is the boundary-crossing step. Everything daysRemaining does happens before that, as a pure calculation.
Calling a pure function from inside an effectful one does not make the pure function itself effectful — daysRemaining behaves identically whether or not main ever calls it.
main's type is IO (), and print is a standard Prelude action available without any explicit import; the program does perform an effect, on its last line.

questions.question: Why can report "Naledi" 82 be tested directly at the GHCi prompt, with no main and no putStrLn involved?
options: Because GHCi secretly wraps every expression in an IO action.
Because report is pure: it only builds and returns a String value, so evaluating it needs nothing beyond the two arguments supplied.
Because putStrLn is automatically called behind the scenes whenever GHCi displays a String.
Because report has no type signature, so GHCi treats it specially.
questions.explanation: report's entire job is to compute a String from name and mark. Since it performs no IO itself, GHCi can evaluate it directly and show the resulting value — exactly like circleArea 2 earlier in the lesson.
optionFeedback: Evaluating an expression at the ghci> prompt is not the same as performing an IO action; GHCi shows the value using its own display machinery, not by running putStrLn.
Correct. This is the whole benefit named earlier in the lesson: a pure function 'can be tested without performing input or output.'
putStrLn is not invoked here at all — GHCi's own value-display mechanism is what shows the quoted string "Naledi scored 82".
report does have an explicit signature, String -> Integer -> String, shown right above its definition.

questions.question: In shout = addEmphasis . map toUpper, which function runs first on the input string?
options: addEmphasis
map toUpper
Both run at the same time
Neither — shout does not call either function directly
questions.explanation: Composition with (.) runs right to left: (f . g) x means f (g x), so the right-hand function, map toUpper, is applied to the original argument first, and its result is what addEmphasis receives.
optionFeedback: addEmphasis is the left-hand, outer function — it runs last, on whatever map toUpper has already produced.
Correct. (.) evaluates its right-hand argument first; that is exactly what 'read f . g from right to left' means.
Haskell evaluates one function at a time here; map toUpper's result becomes addEmphasis's argument, in that order.
shout is defined entirely in terms of these two composed functions — calling shout "..." does call both, just not simultaneously.

questions.question: hasManyWords = (> 3) . length . words is applied to "Short sentence". What does it evaluate to, and why?
options: True, because the string is non-empty
False, because words gives 2 words, length gives 2, and 2 > 3 is False
True, because length counts characters, not words, and there are more than 3 characters
It is a type error, because (> 3) cannot be composed with length
questions.explanation: words "Short sentence" is ["Short","sentence"], a two-element list. length of that list is 2. (> 3) 2 is False. Each stage feeds the next exactly as the right-to-left reading describes.
optionFeedback: Non-emptiness is not what (> 3) . length . words tests; it specifically counts words and compares that count to 3.
Correct. Trace it stage by stage: words splits into 2 words, length counts 2, and 2 is not greater than 3.
length here is applied to the list of words produced by words, not to the original string — it counts words, not characters.
The types line up correctly: words :: String -> [String], length :: [String] -> Int, and (> 3) :: Int -> Bool — this composes and type-checks cleanly.

deeper-reasoning-pure-cores-and-effectfu.title: Deeper reasoning: pure cores and effectful boundaries

questions.question: A classmate reviews the program below and says: "Because this program prints, everything in it is impure, so I can only test scoreLabel by running the whole program and reading the terminal." Which reply gives the most accurate account of where the effect is and how scoreLabel can be checked?
code: scoreLabel s = if s >= 50 then "Pass" else "Fail"
options: The classmate is right. Once a program contains a main, every function it calls becomes effectful, so the only reliable test is to run main and compare the printed line.
scoreLabel is pure only because it has a type signature. If the signature were deleted, scoreLabel would silently become effectful and would have to be tested through main.

Only the call to print performs an effect. scoreLabel's result depends solely on its argument, so it can be evaluated on its own at the GHCi prompt, for example scoreLabel 50, without running main; even map scoreLabel marks is a pure calculation until print displays it.
The line let marks = [72, 45, 50] is the real effect, because it creates data that the rest of the program depends on, so scoreLabel cannot be separated from it.
questions.explanation: Purity is a property of each function's own definition, not of the program that happens to call it. scoreLabel reads nothing and writes nothing, so GHCi can evaluate scoreLabel 50 directly and show "Pass". The only boundary-crossing step is print, which turns the already-computed list into terminal output.
optionFeedback: This treats effects as contagious in the wrong direction. A pure function stays pure when an effectful main calls it; scoreLabel behaves identically whether or not main exists.

Type signatures document and check a function; they do not decide whether it is pure. Deleting scoreLabel's signature changes nothing about its behaviour, and GHC would infer a numeric-comparison type for it instead.
Correct. The effect sits at the boundary (print), the calculation sits in the pure core (scoreLabel and map), and the pure part can be tested without the boundary.
A let binding in a do block just names a value; it reads from nothing outside the program and writes nothing. It is not an effect, and scoreLabel does not depend on it at all.

questions.question: A teammate argues: "Haskell values can never change, so a Haskell program could never track something like a bank balance that goes up and down as deposits arrive." Which response best separates what immutability forbids from what it still allows?
options: Immutability forbids silently overwriting an existing value in place. It does not forbid new information: a deposit produces a new balance value, for example newBalance = addDeposit oldBalance 200, and the old value is still available for checking or undoing.
The teammate is right. Haskell can only model constants, so any changing quantity has to be handled by a program written in another language.
Immutability applies only to numbers. A balance stored in a list or a record can be changed in place, so the teammate's concern does not arise for structured data.
Haskell avoids the issue by treating every deposit as an effect, which means no calculation involving a balance can ever be pure.
questions.explanation: Immutability is about not secretly altering an existing pure value. Change over time is modelled by producing a new value from the old one. The program can still receive new information from the outside world; what it cannot do is have a value that was already bound quietly turn into a different one.
optionFeedback: Correct. The balance "changing" is really a new value derived from the previous one, which also makes the history easy to inspect, test, and reason about.
Haskell programs routinely model counters, balances, and game states; they do it by passing new values forward instead of overwriting old ones.
Immutability applies to Haskell values in general, including lists and records; there is no special in-place exception for structured data.
Reading a new deposit amount from the user is an effect, but computing a new balance from two known numbers is an ordinary pure calculation, so the two jobs stay separate.

questions.question: Both designs below print the same line. A lecturer says the report text must now also be written to a file and checked automatically against an expected string. Which evaluation of the two designs is most accurate?
code: report name mark = putStrLn (name ++ " scored " ++ show mark)
reportText name mark = name ++ " scored " ++ show mark
options: Design A is easier to extend, because putStrLn is inside the function and everything about the report lives in one place.
The two designs are equivalent: any function that returns a value can be turned into one that prints with no loss of testability, because tests can always read the terminal.
Design B is better, but only because it is shorter; length is the real reason pure code is easier to maintain.

Design B is better, because it keeps building the text pure. The same String can be handed to putStrLn, to writeFile, or compared with an expected value in a test, whereas Design A fuses construction and display, so its text can only be observed by running terminal output.
questions.explanation: Design A returns IO (), an action with no usable result, so the text it built is locked inside the print. Design B returns the String itself, a value that any later step can display, store, or test. Separating the pure calculation from the effect is what makes the new requirements cheap.
optionFeedback: Having everything in one place is convenient, but it is exactly what couples the text to the terminal. A function that returns IO () gives the new file-writing and testing requirements nothing to work with.
The designs are not equivalent. A String can be compared with an expected String in one line of code; an IO () action can only be run, with its output captured elsewhere.
Length has nothing to do with it. The advantage comes from the type: reportText returns a value that can be reused, while report returns only an action.
Correct. The benefit is reuse and testability, and it comes directly from keeping the calculation pure and the effect at the boundary.
